old: meadow of asphodel where dwell the souls and shadows
new: meadow of asphodel where the souls and shadows dwell
reason: Inverted archaic word order ('where dwell the souls') forces a listener to hold the subject until after the verb. Also 'asphodel' is an unexplained plant name, but context ('souls and shadows... who can labor no more') makes the meadow's meaning clear enough on its own, so this is a style note, not a comprehension blocker.

old: mighty in your might
new: mighty even in death
reason: Redundant doubling ('mighty in your might') reads as an odd, repetitive tic aloud rather than emphatic; a listener may momentarily wonder if it's a mistake or missed word.

old: The daughters of the old man of the sea
new: The sea-nymphs, daughters of the old sea god
reason: "The old man of the sea" (Nereus) is never named or explained; a listener has to infer from 'daughters' plus the earlier mention of nymphs that this is a sea deity, not a random old man.

old: many a fat sheep and many an ox we sacrificed around you
new: we sacrificed many a fat sheep and many an ox around you
reason: Object-subject-verb inversion ('many a fat sheep... we sacrificed') is archaic syntax that a listener must mentally reorder to parse who is doing the sacrificing.

old: Over these the host of the Argives built a noble tomb
new: Over the bones the host of the Argives built a noble tomb
reason: The paragraph opens on 'Over these,' but its antecedent ('your bleached bones') is in the previous paragraph. Across a paragraph break, an audio listener has likely lost that referent and won't know what 'these' points to.

old: did your enemies make an end of you on the mainland
new: did your enemies kill you on the mainland
reason: "Make an end of you" is an archaic euphemism for killing; a modern listener can work it out from context but it costs a beat of processing.

old: would not say outright that she would not marry
new: would neither refuse to marry again nor agree to it
reason: Double negative construction ('would not say... that she would not marry') is genuinely hard to parse by ear; a listener may come away with the opposite of the intended meaning (that she flatly refused) rather than the intended ambiguity.

old: against the time when death takes him
new: for the time when he dies
reason: "Against" used to mean "in preparation for" is an archaic sense; a modern listener's first read of "against" is opposition, which briefly misdirects the sentence.

old: and they fell thick on one another
new: and the suitors fell in heaps, one on another
reason: "They" is ambiguous here — it could mean the arrows just described or the suitors being struck. A listener has no way to resolve which noun "they" resumes without re-reading.

old: endowed with such rare excellence of understanding
new: so wise and so exceptional
reason: Stiff, formal phrasing ('endowed with... excellence of understanding') is unnatural spoken English and slows the listener down without adding clarity.

old: the daughter of Tyndareus, who killed her lawful husband
new: Clytemnestra, the daughter of Tyndareus, who killed her lawful husband
reason: Clytemnestra is referred to only by patronymic here, several paragraphs removed from the earlier mention of Agamemnon's "wicked wife." A listener can still follow that this is a wife who killed her husband, but the identity is left to inference rather than stated.

old: an old Sicel woman who looked after him
new: an old Sicilian woman who looked after him
reason: "Sicel" (a Sicilian) is an obscure ethnonym never explained; most listeners won't recognize the term, though it doesn't block following the scene.

old: never yet did any stranger come to me whom I liked better
new: no stranger who ever came to me pleased me more
reason: "Never yet did any stranger come" is an inverted, archaic construction a listener must untangle to find the subject and verb.

old: Neither his mother, nor I his father, who were his parents, could throw our arms about him
new: Neither his mother nor I, his father, could throw our arms about him
reason: A triple-stacked negative/relative construction ('Neither... nor I... who were his parents, could') is very hard to track by ear; the redundant 'who were his parents' clause (restating what 'his mother' and 'I his father' already establish) adds to the tangle rather than clarifying it.

old: The birds all flew on our right hands
new: The birds all flew on our right — a sign of good luck
reason: Bird-omen divination (favorable birds flying to the right) is never explained; a listener unfamiliar with the convention will register it as an odd, meaningless detail rather than the good omen the surrounding lines describe.

old: his nostrils quivered
new: his breath caught
reason: An isolated physical detail ('nostrils quivered') with no other emotional cue reads oddly out of context aloud; a listener may not immediately connect it to Odysseus's grief.

old: the gifts which, when he was over here, he had promised to give me
new: the gifts he had promised to give me when he was here
reason: The interrupting clause ('when he was over here') splits the relative clause from its verb, making the sentence harder to follow by ear than necessary.

old: when heaven’s heat has been laid heavy upon them
new: when the summer sun has ripened them
reason: Poetic archaic phrasing for "when the sun ripens them"; a listener can guess the gist but the literal image (heat "laid heavy") is not immediately parseable.

old: the cities of the Cephallenians
new: the cities of Ithaca and the nearby islands
reason: "Cephallenians" (the people under Odysseus's rule) is never explained and recurs later in the Book (also in this paragraph's counterpart at paragraph 28) without clarification; a listener isn't told this is essentially the people of Ithaca and its neighboring islands.

old: Would that, by Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, I were the man I was
new: If only, by Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, I were the man I once was
reason: "Would that...I were" is an archaic optative-wish construction not used in ordinary spoken English; understandable from context but noticeably stilted aloud.

old: If I were still what I then was and had been in our house yesterday
new: If I were still the man I once was and had been in our house yesterday
reason: "What I then was" repeats the idea just stated ("the man I was") in an awkward, circular phrasing that reads as clumsy rather than emphatic.

old: took each his proper place on the benches and seats
new: each took his proper place on the benches and seats
reason: Inverted word order ('took each his proper place') is archaic syntax; the ordinary English order ('each took his place') is immediately clear.

old: buried every man his own
new: each man buried his own dead
reason: Archaic inverted phrasing ('buried every man his own') omits the implied object and reorders subject/verb, making the sentence genuinely hard to parse by ear on first hearing.

old: Let us be up and doing before he can get away
new: Let us act now, before he can get away
reason: "Be up and doing" is a dated idiom for taking action; a listener can infer the meaning but it's not natural contemporary phrasing.

old: Let us be up, then, and after them
new: Let us move, then, and go after them
reason: Elliptical archaic phrasing ('be up... and after them') drops the verb of pursuit; understandable in context but not natural spoken English.

old: in the wantonness of their hearts
new: in their reckless self-indulgence
reason: "Wantonness of their hearts" is archaic, poetic diction; a modern listener will likely need to guess at the meaning (reckless self-indulgence) from context alone.

old: down she darted from the highest peaks of Olympus
new: she darted down from the highest peaks of Olympus
reason: Inverted word order ('down she darted') is archaic syntax; ordinary order reads immediately clearly.

old: All hail, therefore, and may the gods prosper you
new: Welcome home, then, and may the gods prosper you
reason: "All hail" is an archaic greeting/exclamation not used in contemporary English and may momentarily strike a listener as a formal salute rather than a warm greeting.

old: and you shall see, if you will, that I am in no mind to disgrace your family
new: and you will see that I have no intention of disgracing your family
reason: The cluster of archaic forms ('shall see,' 'if you will,' 'in no mind to') stacks three dated constructions in one clause, making it read stiffly rather than as natural filial reassurance.

old: pray to the gray-eyed maiden
new: pray to gray-eyed Athena
reason: Athena, disguised as Mentor, tells Laertes to pray to "the gray-eyed maiden" — an epithet for herself — without any signal that she means herself. A first-time listener, hearing Mentor's voice, has no way to know this epithet refers to the very figure speaking; the confusion is confirmed moments later when the narration says Laertes "prayed to her."

old: for the helmet did not stay it
new: for the helmet did not stop it
reason: "Stay" meaning "to stop/halt" is an archaic sense; a modern listener's default reading of "stay" (remain in place) briefly produces the wrong image before the sentence's logic corrects it.

old: So spoke Athena, and Odysseus obeyed her gladly
new: Athena spoke, and Odysseus obeyed her gladly
reason: Inverted "So spoke [subject]" is archaic narrative syntax; ordinary subject-verb order is clearer and this construction recurs across the Book (see paragraph 5, "So he spoke") without ever settling into a felt convention for a first-time listener.
